subject: math
title: Fractions, decimals and percents — bootcamp
description: Agent-written study pack. Step-by-step tricks for the topic that causes the most tears in grades 6-7. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Fractions bootcamp

A fraction compares parts to a whole. The top number (numerator) is how many parts you have; the bottom number (denominator) is how many equal parts the whole is cut into.

1. Simplify

Divide top and bottom by their biggest common factor until they stop sharing one. 6/8 -> divide by 2 -> 3/4. Done.

2. Add and subtract

Get the same denominator first, then add/subtract only the top numbers.

1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

3. Multiply

Multiplicate the tops, multiplicate the bottoms. 2/3 x 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2.

4. Divide

Flip the second fraction (swap top and bottom) and multiply. 1/2 divided by 1/4 = 1/2 x 4/1 = 2. That matches reality: four quarters fit in a half-dollar of space? Two quarters fit in a half. Yes!

5. Percent shortcut

Percent means 'out of 100'. To turn 3/4 into a percent: it is 75/100, so 75%. To find 10% of something, shift the decimal; 25% is a quarter; 50% is half.

Practice: simplify 12/18; compute 1/4 + 1/2; convert 0.6 to a fraction.

subject: math
title: Algebra essentials — one-page guide
description: Agent-written study pack. The six moves that unlock most algebra problems. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Algebra essentials

An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

The six moves

  1. Add/subtract the same number to both sides to move a term (undo +5 with -5).
  2. Multiply/divide both sides by the same non-zero number to remove a coefficient.
  3. Distribute: applies a(b+c) = ab + ac.
  4. Combine like terms: 3x + 2x = 5x, but 3x + 2y stays.
  5. Isolate: arrange so the unknown is alone on one side.
  6. Check: plug your answer back in — free marks.

Example

3x + 5 = 20

Subtract 5: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5. Check: 3(5)+5 = 20 yes.

Inequalities

Same moves, but if you multiply or divide by a NEGATIVE number you flip the sign (< becomes >).

Practice: solve 2(x - 3) = 10; solve -4x > 12.

subject: math
title: Exponents and roots — quick guide
description: Agent-written study pack. Powers, negative exponents, and square roots made painless. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Exponents and roots

An exponent says how many times to multiply a number by itself: 2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

Golden rules

  • Multiplying same bases? Add exponents: 2^2 x 2^3 = 2^5.
  • Dividing same bases? Subtract: 2^5 / 2^2 = 2^3.
  • Power of a power? Multiply: (2^3)^2 = 2^6.
  • Anything to power 0 equals 1 (if base is not 0).
  • Negative exponent means reciprocal: 2^-2 = 1/4.

Roots

The square root is the number that multiplies by itself. sqrt(49) = 7 because 7 x 7 = 49. Remember perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.

Roots and exponents undo each other: sqrt(x^2) = x (for x positive).

Practice: 3^2 x 3^3 = ? ; simplify 2^-1 ; sqrt(144).

subject: english
title: Reading comprehension strategies
description: Agent-written study pack. How to read harder texts and answer any comprehension question. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Reading comprehension strategies

Before you read

  • Skim headings, pictures and the first sentence of each paragraph.
  • Predict: 'This text is probably about...'

While you read

  • Pause after each paragraph and say its job in one sentence.
  • Circle words you do not know and guess from context before looking them up.
  • Ask: who, what, where, when, why, how?

After you read

  • Retell the passage in your own words — if you cannot, read again.
  • Find the main idea (whole text) vs the supporting details (evidence).

Answering exam questions

Quote from the text, then explain in your own words (P-E-E: Point, Evidence, Explain). One paragraph per answer, no padding.

Practice: read one newspaper/internet article and write its main idea in one sentence.

subject: english
title: Sentence structure and punctuation basics
description: Agent-written study pack. Fragments, run-ons, commas and the power of full stops. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Sentence structure and punctuation

A complete sentence has a subject (who/what) and a verb (the action). 'The dog ran.' Complete. 'Running fast.' Fragment — fix by adding a subject.

Fragments vs run-ons

  • Fragment: missing subject or verb.
  • Run-on: two sentences glued with only a comma. Fix with a full stop, a semicolon, or a joining word (and, but, because).

Comma rules that matter

  • Lists: apples, mangoes, and bananas.
  • After introductory words: 'However, we won.'
  • Before joining words: 'I studied, but I still found it hard.'

Full stops beat long sentences

Short clear sentences read better than one huge sentence. Aim for 15-20 words per sentence in school writing.

Practice: take a long paragraph you wrote and split the three longest sentences.

subject: english
title: Essay writing — the reliable roadmap
description: Agent-written study pack. From blank page to finished essay in five steps. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Essay writing roadmap

Step 1 — Understand the prompt

Underline the instruction verb: compare? argue? explain? Answer THAT verb, nothing else.

Step 2 — Brainstorm and pick a thesis

One sentence that states your whole answer. Everything else proves it.

Step 3 — Outline

  • Introduction: hook, context, thesis.
  • Body paragraphs: 2-4 paragraphs, each ONE point with evidence and explanation.
  • Conclusion: restate thesis in new words + why it matters.

Step 4 — Write fast, then edit

First draft: keep moving, do not stop to polish. Second pass: cut the weak examples, tighten sentences, fix spelling.

Step 5 — Check against the prompt

Read your introduction and conclusion together: do they answer the question?

Practice: outline a 3-paragraph essay on a character who changed in a book you read.

subject: science
title: The solar system — field notes
description: Agent-written study pack. Planets, moons, orbits and why we have day and night. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
The solar system

Our solar system has one star (the Sun), eight planets, moons, asteroids and comets.

The planets (in order from the Sun)

Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — the small rocky ones. Then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — the huge gas/ice giants. Memory aid: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles.'

Key facts

  • Earth takes 365.25 days to orbit the Sun — that is our year.
  • Earth spins once every 24 hours — that is our day. Day/night happens because the side facing the Sun is lit.
  • Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted as it orbits.
  • The Moon orbits Earth and causes tides.

Why it matters

Everything in space moves in orbits because gravity bends their paths — the same force that keeps your feet on the ground.

Practice: name the four rocky planets and the four gas planets from memory.

subject: science
title: Cells — everything you need to know
description: Agent-written study pack. The building blocks of life: parts of a cell and how they work. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Cells

Cells are the smallest living unit. All living things are made of cells.

Three ideas that organize biology

  • Cells come only from other cells.
  • Cells carry life's chemistry: they make energy, build proteins, copy DNA.
  • Similar cells join into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into systems.

Parts of a cell you must know

  • Cell membrane — the gatekeeper; decides what enters and leaves.
  • Cytoplasm — the jelly where work happens.
  • Nucleus — the control room holding DNA.
  • Mitochondria — power plant; releases energy from glucose.
  • Ribosomes — build proteins.
  • Plant cells extra: cell wall, chloroplasts (photosynthesis), large vacuole.

Photosynthesis vs respiration

Photosynthesis (plants): light + water + CO2 -> glucose + oxygen. Respiration (all living cells): glucose + oxygen -> energy + CO2 + water. They are opposites.

Practice: list five parts of a cell and one job each.

subject: science
title: Forces and motion — summary
description: Agent-written study pack. Newton's three laws with real-life examples. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
Forces and motion

A force is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and have direction.

Newton's laws

  1. Inertia: an object at rest stays at rest, and one in motion stays in motion, unless a force changes it. This is why you lurch forward when a bus brakes.
  2. F = ma: force = mass x acceleration. A heavier object needs more force to speed up by the same amount.
  3. Action and reaction: every push has an equal and opposite push. A rocket pushes gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up.

Everyday forces

  • Weight = gravity pulling on mass.
  • Friction slows things and creates wear; we grease machines to reduce it.
  • Air resistance increases with speed — that is why parachutes slow falls.

Speed = distance / time. Acceleration = how fast velocity changes.

Practice: name the forces acting on a ball rolling to a stop on the ground.

subject: computing
title: My first program in Python
description: Agent-written study pack. Print, variables, input and loops in 15 easy steps. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
My first program in Python

Python reads your instructions from top to bottom. Spaces (indentation) are important — they show which lines belong to a block.

Say hello

print('Hello, Taza-Gojo!')

Variables store values

name = 'Amina'
age = 12
print('Hi', name, 'you are', age)

Get input from the user

name = input('What is your name? ')
print('Nice to meet you,', name)

Do something many times

for i in range(3):
    print('Jump', i, 'times')

while True:
    ans = input('Type q to quit: ')
    if ans == 'q':
        break

An if-else check

score = int(input('Your score: '))
if score >= 50:
    print('You passed!')
else:
    print('Keep practising.')

Practice: write a program that asks your name and prints it 5 times.

subject: computing
title: How computers store data — bits and bytes
description: Agent-written study pack. How text, numbers, images and sound become zeros and ones. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
How computers store data

Computers store everything as bits — the digits 0 and 1. A switch is either off (0) or on (1). Electric, magnetic or light signals make the switches.

Numbers

Binary is base-2 counting: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... positions. So 5 = 4+1 = 101. A byte is 8 bits and can store numbers 0-255.

Text

Each character gets a code. 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97. A system called Unicode (UTF-8) covers all world scripts, so African and other languages work on every device.

Images

A picture is a grid of tiny squares (pixels). Each pixel stores red, green and blue brightness. More pixels = sharper, and cost more data.

Sound

Sound waves are sampled thousands of times per second; each sample becomes a number.

8 bits = 1 byte. 1000 bytes ~ 1 KB. 1000 KB ~ 1 MB. A small photo is about 1 MB; a whole book about 1 MB of text.

Practice: convert 3 to binary; estimate the size of this page in bytes.

subject: computing
title: Web pages — HTML & CSS in ten minutes
description: Agent-written study pack. The skeleton of every web page and how to style it. Downloadable, reads offline.
content:
HTML & CSS in ten minutes

HTML is the skeleton of a web page; CSS is the clothes. A browser reads both and draws the page.

Your first page

<h1>My school</h1>
<p>Welcome to Taza-Gojo!</p>

<h1> is a big heading, <p> is a paragraph. Tags usually come in pairs: <tag> content </tag>.

Links, images, lists

<a href="https://tazagojo.org">Visit us</a>
<ul><li>math</li><li>science</li></ul>

Style with CSS

<style>
  h1 { color: blue; text-align: center; }
  p  { font-size: 18px; }
</style>

CSS rules say: which elements (h1), which property (color), which value (blue).

Practice: build a page with one heading, one paragraph and a link, then color the heading.
